questions.text: Which of the following is the most appropriate title for the passage?
questions.context: Told that a wristband is a genuine antique from a famous historical figure, people report it as more meaningful and are willing to pay considerably more for it than for an identical wristband described as a modern reproduction, even when no physical test could ever distinguish the two objects apart. The object itself has not changed in any measurable way; what has changed is its perceived causal history, its connection to a particular chain of past events. Philosophers call this an object's essentialist value: worth derived not from physical properties but from an invisible, believed-in history behind the object.

options.text: Why Antiques Are Always More Valuable Than Reproductions
Essentialist Value: Why an Object's Believed History Matters More Than Its Properties
How Physical Tests Can Distinguish Genuine Antiques From Reproductions
The Psychology of Wristband Collecting
Why Modern Reproductions Are Indistinguishable From Originals

questions.text: Choose the most appropriate topic of the passage.
questions.context: A single degraded copy of a photograph, repeatedly recopied across generations with each copy made from the previous copy rather than the original, accumulates visible degradation far faster than a single copy made directly from a well-preserved original would. Digital information faces an analogous risk from format obsolescence rather than physical degradation: a file saved in a format no current software can open is, for practical purposes, as lost as data on a decayed physical medium, regardless of how perfectly the underlying bits themselves have been preserved. Archivists therefore treat active format migration, not simply storage, as essential to genuine long-term preservation.

options.text: why photographs degrade more quickly than digital files
how format obsolescence threatens digital preservation as seriously as physical decay threatens photographs
techniques for repairing a degraded photographic copy
the total storage capacity required for archiving digital files
why archivists prefer physical media over digital storage

questions.text: Choose the most appropriate topic of the passage.
questions.context: Termite mounds, some rising several metres above the surrounding savannah, maintain remarkably stable internal temperatures and humidity despite extreme swings in outside conditions, achieved entirely through the mound's passive architecture rather than any active climate control by the termites themselves. A network of internal chimneys and tunnels drives continuous air circulation, drawing warm, stale air upward and out while pulling cooler air in near the base, powered by nothing more than temperature differences between the mound's interior and the surrounding air. Architects studying the design have adapted similar passive-ventilation principles for buildings that maintain comfortable temperatures using drastically less energy than conventional air conditioning requires.

options.text: the total height that termite mounds can reach
how a termite mound's passive architecture regulates temperature without active climate control
the diet and foraging behaviour of termite colonies
why savannah temperatures fluctuate more than other climates
methods architects use to demolish outdated buildings

questions.text: Which of the following best states the main point of the passage?
questions.context: A translator working between two languages with fundamentally different grammatical structures for describing time and causation often finds that certain thoughts, easily expressed in one language, resist natural expression in the other without extensive rephrasing, not because the target language lacks the vocabulary but because its grammar simply does not carve up events the same way. This has led some researchers to argue that the language a person habitually thinks in may subtly shape which distinctions feel natural to draw at all, without making any distinction literally impossible to express with enough effort.

options.text: Some languages are objectively more sophisticated than others at describing time and causation.
The grammar of a person's habitual language may subtly shape which distinctions feel natural, without making other distinctions impossible.
Translators should avoid working between languages with different grammatical structures.
Certain thoughts are permanently impossible to express in some languages, regardless of effort.
Vocabulary differences, not grammar, are the primary source of translation difficulty.

questions.text: How many of the statements below do NOT agree with the passage?
questions.context:
For most of my twenties, I treated every piece of critical feedback on my writing as evidence I should quit, and would avoid showing anyone a draft until it felt completely finished, by which point revising it felt like undoing all the work I had already done. An editor I worked with briefly gave me one piece of advice that actually changed things: share a draft you know is unfinished and rough, specifically so that feedback arrives while revision still feels natural rather than like demolition. I still find early feedback uncomfortable to receive. What changed is that I now share drafts roughly three times earlier in the process than I used to, and the discomfort no longer stops me from doing it.

Statements
(a) The writer used to treat critical feedback as a signal that she should quit writing.
(b) She used to wait until a draft felt completely finished before sharing it.
(c) The editor advised sharing a draft only once it felt entirely polished.
(d) She no longer finds early feedback uncomfortable to receive.
(e) She now shares drafts earlier in her process than she previously did.
(f) The discomfort of early feedback no longer prevents her from sharing drafts.

questions.text: Which statement does NOT agree with the two explanations given in the passage?
questions.context: Salmon return, after years spent at sea, to spawn in the specific freshwater stream where they themselves hatched, navigating hundreds of kilometres of open ocean to find it. One explanation holds that salmon imprint on their home stream's distinctive chemical signature as juveniles, before migrating to sea, and recognise this signature again upon returning, using it to guide the final stages of the journey. A second, competing explanation emphasises magnetic sensitivity: salmon may register the specific geomagnetic signature of their home stream's location and navigate toward that magnetic coordinate across the open ocean, well before any chemical cue could possibly be detected.

options.text: The first explanation attributes stream recognition to a chemical signature imprinted during the juvenile stage.
The first explanation suggests salmon recognise the chemical cue only upon returning to fresh water.
The second explanation attributes long-distance ocean navigation to sensitivity to geomagnetic signatures.
The second explanation agrees with the first that chemical imprinting guides navigation across the entire ocean journey.
Both explanations attempt to account for the same observed homing behaviour.

questions.text: Which of the following best explains the meaning of the underlined phrase "the illusion of explanatory depth"?
questions.context: Asked to rate how well they understand how a bicycle's gears work, most people respond confidently, but when subsequently asked to actually explain the mechanism step by step, their confidence collapses almost immediately, and the explanation they produce is noticeably thinner than their initial rating suggested. Researchers call this _the illusion of explanatory depth_: a sense of understanding borrowed from having seen a mechanism function reliably many times, mistaken for genuine comprehension of why it functions at all.

options.text: a genuine, deep understanding of mechanical systems that most people already possess
a false sense of understanding that collapses once a person is asked to actually explain the mechanism
a preference for simple mechanisms over genuinely complex ones
the fact that bicycles are more mechanically complex than most people realise
a bias that only affects people with no mechanical experience whatsoever

questions.text: Which of the following questions CANNOT be answered from the passage?
questions.context: Cuttlefish can alter both the colour and texture of their skin within a fraction of a second, using specialised pigment cells called chromatophores that expand and contract under direct neural control, entirely bypassing the slower hormonal pathways most other camouflaging animals rely on. Remarkably, cuttlefish themselves are colour-blind, which has led researchers to a competing hypothesis: photoreceptor cells embedded directly in the skin may allow the animal to sense light and colour information without routing it through the eyes at all, though this remains only partly confirmed. A startled cuttlefish can also rapidly raise small skin projections called papillae to mimic the rough texture of coral or rock.

options.text: What structures allow a cuttlefish to change its skin colour so quickly?
Is the mechanism behind cuttlefish colour-matching fully confirmed by researchers?
How many distinct skin colours can a cuttlefish produce simultaneously?
What is one hypothesis for how a colour-blind cuttlefish detects colour information?
What additional change can a startled cuttlefish make to its skin besides colour?

questions.text: How many of the underlined parts are grammatically INCORRECT?
questions.context: The sunk cost fallacy describes a pattern in which people continue investing in a failing course of action because of resources already spent, rather than resources likely to be gained going forward. ① _A company that has spent heavily on a failing product line often continue funding it well past the point a fresh evaluation would recommend._ ② _Behavioural economists attribute this partly to a reluctance to publicly acknowledge that prior spending was, in effect, wasted._ ③ _The same pattern extend to personal decisions, such as finishing a boring book solely because of the hours already invested in it._ ④ _Rationally, only future costs and benefits should influence a decision going forward, regardless of what has already been spent._ ⑤ _Recognising the fallacy explicitly, some evidence suggests, modestly improves people's ability to resist it in subsequent decisions._

questions.text: Which underlined part is grammatically incorrect?
questions.context: The availability heuristic ① _describes_ a tendency to judge the likelihood of an event by how easily examples of it come to mind, rather than by its actual statistical frequency. Vivid, heavily reported events such as plane crashes ② _are recalled_ far more easily than statistically more common but less dramatic risks, such as routine car accidents. This mismatch between vividness and actual frequency ③ _lead_ people to systematically overestimate rare, dramatic risks while underestimating common, mundane ones. Insurance purchasing patterns ④ _reflect_ this bias clearly, with sales of disaster coverage spiking noticeably after a widely reported disaster elsewhere. Awareness of the heuristic ⑤ _does not reliably eliminate_ its influence on judgement.

the measure itself becomes the object of direct optimisation, diverging from the broader goal it was meant to represent

questions.context: Slime moulds, single-celled organisms with no brain or nervous system whatsoever, can solve surprisingly sophisticated spatial problems, such as finding the shortest path through a maze toward a food source. ① Researchers placed oat flakes at locations corresponding to major cities on a map and allowed a slime mould to grow between them inside a miniature replica of the surrounding terrain. ② The resulting network of the mould's tendrils closely resembled the actual layout of an existing regional rail network, built by human engineers over decades. ③ Slime moulds reproduce through spores that can remain dormant for years under unfavourable conditions. ④ The mould appears to solve the problem through a simple, local process of reinforcing efficient connections and withdrawing from inefficient ones, with no central planning of any kind. ⑤ This suggests that sophisticated network optimisation does not necessarily require anything resembling a brain to emerge.

questions.context: Participants asked to taste and rate an identical wine sample rate it more favourably when told it costs ninety dollars than when told the same wine costs ten dollars. ( ① ) Brain imaging conducted during tasting shows measurably greater activity in pleasure-related regions for the "expensive" sample, not merely a difference in the rating participants later report. ( ② ) This suggests the price is altering the actual sensory experience itself, not simply biasing participants' willingness to admit disliking an "expensive" product. questions.text:
Choose the most appropriate place for the given sentence.

questions.context: In the years leading up to a major market downturn, financial commentators frequently described a "new era" of permanently higher valuations, arguing that traditional measures of a company's worth no longer applied to a transformed economy. ( ① ) Such claims tend to recur, in slightly different language, before nearly every major speculative bubble in recorded financial history. ( ② ) Investors who might otherwise have been cautious found the "this time is different" argument persuasive precisely because each specific version was tailored to that era's genuinely novel circumstances. ( ③ ) Skeptical voices warning that valuations remained fundamentally tethered to ordinary economic principles were routinely dismissed as failing to understand the new landscape. ( ④ ) The pattern's persistence across otherwise very different historical episodes suggests something structural about how bubbles are rationalised while they are still inflating. ( ⑤ )

(A) Return rates, measured by the percentage of borrowed items eventually returned at all, actually improved slightly after fees were removed, since patrons no longer avoided the library altogether once a fine had accumulated past what they felt able to pay.
(B) Librarians had long assumed late fees were necessary to encourage timely returns, and worried that eliminating them entirely would result in significantly more books never being returned at all.

A wetland positioned between farmland and a river performs a filtering function that would otherwise require expensive engineered infrastructure.

(A) Excess nitrogen and phosphorus from agricultural runoff are absorbed and processed by wetland plants and soil microbes before the water ever reaches the river's main channel.
(B) Removing a wetland to expand farmland, therefore, does not merely eliminate habitat; it removes a filtering function whose engineered replacement can cost far more than the value of the reclaimed land.
(C) Without this filtering step, the same nutrients would flow directly into the river, feeding the kind of algal blooms that starve river ecosystems of oxygen downstream.

Arrange sentences ①–⑤ so that they fit the passage. Which sentence should come fourth?

Negotiation researchers distinguish between distributive bargaining, in which one party's gain is necessarily the other's loss, and integrative bargaining, in which both parties can gain simultaneously.

① Distributive bargaining suits situations genuinely limited to a single, fixed resource being divided between two parties, such as agreeing on a single sale price for an existing object.
② Integrative bargaining becomes possible whenever the two parties value different aspects of a deal differently, allowing trades that leave both sides better off than a simple fixed split would.
③ A common mistake is treating every negotiation as distributive by default, searching only for a fair split rather than exploring whether trades exist that could benefit both sides.
④ Skilled negotiators therefore begin by identifying which parts of a negotiation are genuinely fixed and which parts allow for value-creating trades before settling into a purely competitive stance.
⑤ Treating an integrative opportunity as if it were purely distributive, in other words, can leave real, mutually beneficial value unclaimed on the table.
